messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina was a 21-year-old African American woman who had come to treatment after months of feeling as if the combat zone had followed her home. She had served in a support role overseas, and the event she kept returning to involved a night convoy that was suddenly swept into confusion when helicopters came low overhead and gunfire broke out nearby. In the chaos, a series of decisions she made felt to her like the moment everything changed; she was the one who had been responsible for keeping others calm and moving, and ever since, she had been haunted by the conviction that something about her made the attack possible. She would replay the scene in fragments, especially the sound of aircraft or helicopters passing over her apartment in the city, and even a dark hallway at night could bring back the same surge of dread she felt while waiting for the next blast. When family members asked casual questions about “what happened over there,” or when someone mentioned their own family as a source of support, Amina felt a sharp tightening in her chest, as if the conversation itself were opening the door to the worst night of her life. In those moments she became certain that another person would not have ended up trapped in that situation, and she turned the blame inward, telling herself that there was something about her that made the event happen.

Over time, those reminders began to shape the narrow way she moved through her life. She started avoiding people she had socialized with before the deployment, even friends who had known her for years, because seeing them seemed to press her face-to-face with who she had been before she changed. She no longer wanted to start new friendships or relationships, not because she did not want closeness, but because closeness felt dangerous and temporary, something that would only expose how unlike her former self she had become. She also stopped watching television programs or films that dealt with war, rescue missions, or similar disasters, and she refused to read news stories that might carry images or descriptions that echoed the convoy attack. As these routines settled in, they brought their own painful evidence. At work, where she was employed as a counselor, she found herself less able to do the things that had once defined her: she hesitated in sessions, doubted her instincts, and quietly concluded that she was no longer capable of being the steady, competent helper she had believed herself to be. The more she withdrew from coworkers, old friends, and any possibility of new attachment, the more she was left alone with the conviction that someone else would not have gotten into this situation, and that if she had been stronger or smarter, none of this would have happened. Her avoidance seemed to confirm the very judgments that drove it, narrowing her life until the losses felt like proof.

That shrinking world also made the reminders harder to escape. Because she kept away from friends, she no longer had the buffering familiarity of their company when a helicopter passed overhead or when a neighbor’s comment about “family back home” cut unexpectedly close. Because she avoided films and news, the few times she did encounter a similar scene—some dark footage on a screen in a waiting room, a documentary playing in a shared space—felt even more jarring, arriving without warning and leaving her flooded with the same shame and alarm. The more she stayed away from those situations, the more potent each reminder became, and the more readily she returned to the thought that there was something in her that made disaster find her. That belief, in turn, made it even harder for her to reach out to people, since if she was somehow the reason things went wrong, it made sense to keep others at a distance rather than risk disappointing them or pulling them into her distress. What had begun as an attempt to protect herself gradually made every trigger feel closer, louder, and more unavoidable.

By the time she sought help, Amina was exhausted by the effort of keeping her life small and controlled. She still worked, but the role that once gave her identity now felt brittle and uncertain, and she was frightened by how quickly a sound from the sky or a darkened corridor could pull her back into the convoy night. What brought her in was the fear that she was becoming permanently unlike the person she had been, and that if she continued this way she would lose not only her confidence but her ability to connect at all. More than anything, she hoped to stop believing that she was the one who caused it, and to find out whether she could ever feel capable, and safe, enough to let other people near again.
